prompt.context: Our client is Magna Health, a health care company in the Midwest. It both insures patients and provides health care services. Employers pay a fixed premium to Magna for each of their employees in return for which Magna covers all necessary health services of the employee (ranging from physician care, and medications to hospitalization). Magna currently has 300,000 patients enrolled in its plan. It has 300 salaried physician employees who provide a broad range of services to patients in 6 centers. These physicians represent a wide range of specialty areas, but not all areas. When a patient needs medical treatment in a specialty area not covered by a Magna physician, they are referred outside of the Magna network for care, and Magna pays all referral costs on a fee-for-service basis. Magna doesn't own any hospitals itself, instead contracting services from several local hospitals. Over the past six months, Magna has been experiencing declining profitability. Magna's CEO has retained McKinsey to help determine what is causing the problem and how Magna might fix it.
prompt.question: How can Magna Health improve its financial situation?

clarifying_info.q: Has Magna's subscriber base changed recently?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — the demographics have shifted significantly over the past 5 years, from majority industrial workers/laborers to majority office employees.

clarifying_info.q: What is the prevalence rate of serious heart disease in Magna's patient population?
clarifying_info.a: The prevalence rate of serious heart disease in the 65+ population is 30 percent; in the under-65 population it is 10 percent.

clarifying_info.q: What does a single cardiology referral cost Magna?
clarifying_info.a: The cost of a cardiology referral is $200.

framework: Revenues: premium price per employee and number of employees covered
Medical costs: hospital, drugs, outpatient care
Outpatient costs: internal physician costs vs. external referral costs
Patient base demographics and overall risk profile affecting medical costs

questions.prompt: The demographics of Magna's subscribers have changed significantly over the past 5 years, from majority industrial workers/laborers to majority office employees. Knowing this, what specific areas would you investigate first?
questions.guidance: Claim costs — the shift in subscriber base changes the disease profile (more heart disease/stress, less work-related injury). External referral costs — the change in disease profile affects which specialties Magna has in-house competency for.

questions.prompt: Your team has gathered the following data: Magna Health has 300,000 patients and an average referral cost of $20 per member per month; Sunshine HMO has 500,000 patients and an average referral cost of $15 per member per month. What are the most likely reasons that Magna's average referral cost is higher than Sunshine's?
questions.guidance: Referral pricing: Magna may be paying more than Sunshine for specialist services (higher contract rates). Number of referrals: Magna physicians may have different practice patterns and refer more frequently. Mix of specialties: Magna's referral specialties (e.g., cardiology, neurosurgery) may be more expensive than Sunshine's (e.g., cardiology, psychiatry). Mix of patients: Magna may have sicker or older (65+) patients who need more specialist care.

questions.prompt: What analyses would you conduct to investigate the referral cost drivers you identified?
questions.guidance: Referral pricing: obtain Magna's prices for common specialties; compare to competitor/industry averages via specialist interviews. Number of referrals: interview Magna and non-Magna physicians for behavioral differences; consult industry publications. Mix of specialties: compare referral counts by specialty for Magna and Sunshine. Mix of patients: compare demographic data for Magna and Sunshine; check whether Magna's referral cost increase tracks its demographic shift.

questions.prompt: Magna's CEO wants to know how many cardiology referrals Magna should expect annually given its patient population. Assume: 300,000 total patients; 20% are age 65 or older; patients with serious heart disease visit cardiologists an average of 5 times per year. (You should ask for prevalence rates.)
questions.guidance: Segment patients into 65+ and under-65 groups, apply the respective prevalence rates to get the number of patients with serious heart disease, then multiply each by 5 annual visits and sum.

math.setup: Split patients by age band; apply heart-disease prevalence to each band; multiply by 5 visits/year.
steps: 60,000 x 30% prevalence = 18,000 patients age 65+ with serious heart disease
240,000 x 10% prevalence = 24,000 patients under 65 with serious heart disease
24,000 x 5 visits = 120,000 referrals/year from under-65 group
90,000 + 120,000 = 210,000 total expected cardiology referrals per year

questions.prompt: Magna's CEO reveals that Magna actually pays for 300,000 annual cardiology referrals — far above the expected 210,000. Why might actual referrals be significantly higher than the U.S. average? How would you verify the causes?
questions.guidance: Higher-than-average heart-disease prevalence in Magna's population — audit internal data and compare to U.S. national figures. PCPs referring patients who do not have serious heart disease — interview specialists or track a sample of referred patients. PCP discomfort or lack of training treating cardiac patients (malpractice avoidance) — interview Magna physicians; conduct external review. Absence of clear referral guidelines or non-compliance — obtain expert opinion on current guidelines. No incentives or penalties to limit unnecessary referrals — review incentive schemes; benchmark against comparable programs.

questions.prompt: Magna will pilot an incentive plan: (1) $100,000 bonuses to each of the 10 primary care physicians with the lowest cardiac referral rates consistent with good outcomes; (2) overall fee increases totaling $1 million to handle more basic cardiology in-house. Assuming a referral cost of $200 and 300,000 current annual referrals, how many fewer referrals does Magna need to recoup the cost of the plan?
questions.guidance: Calculate total incentive cost, then divide by the savings per referral avoided.

math.setup: Total incentive cost = bonus pool + fee increase. Break-even referral reduction = total cost / cost per referral.
steps: Break-even referrals to cut: $2,000,000 / $200 per referral = 10,000 referrals
math.answer: 10,000 fewer referrals (a 3.3% reduction) to break even

questions.prompt: Your team projects the incentive plan will reduce referrals by 5% in year 1 and an additional 2% in year 2. By how much would Magna's referral costs be reduced over the two-year period?
questions.guidance: Year 1: apply 5% reduction to 300,000 referrals. Year 2: apply 2% reduction to the reduced base (285,000). Sum both years' savings.

math.setup: Year 1 savings: 5% of 300,000 referrals x $200. Year 2 savings: 2% of 285,000 referrals x $200. Total = Year 1 + Year 2.
math.answer: $3.0 million in year 1; $4.14 million in year 2; $7.14 million total over two years

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the cardiac financial incentive program, what other ideas should Magna consider to reduce the cost of specialist referrals?

categories.name: Change physician behavior
ideas: Provide training on treating patients with minor or stable medical conditions
Define and clarify medical guidelines for referrals (e.g., committee defining 'serious' vs. 'minor' heart disease)
Institute a peer review committee to approve high-cost referrals

categories.name: Target outlier physicians
ideas: Identify physicians who refer at much higher rates than peers
Focus improvement efforts on outliers to achieve outsized cost reduction

categories.name: Expand in-house capabilities
ideas: Assess whether bringing cardiology, neurosurgery, or oncology in-house would reduce costs
Evaluate cost-benefit of hiring additional specialists vs. continued external referrals

categories.name: Improve referral contracts
ideas: Review and renegotiate specialist contracts where Magna is paying above-market rates
Benchmark contract rates against Sunshine HMO and industry averages

categories.name: Extend to other specialties
ideas: Apply the same referral-reduction analysis to neurosurgery and other high-cost referral areas
Determine whether cost reduction potential exists beyond cardiology

recommendation: Magna's declining profitability is primarily driven by high medical claims costs, specifically above-average external referral costs — $20 per member per month vs. Sunshine's $15.
The root causes are likely excessive cardiology referrals (300,000 actual vs. 210,000 expected), driven by PCP practice patterns, lack of referral guidelines, and absence of physician incentives.

Recommend piloting the physician incentive plan (estimated 2-year savings of $7.14M against a $2M cost) while simultaneously addressing referral guidelines, PCP training, and specialist contract rates.
risks: Physician resistance or unintended quality-of-care compromises from financial incentives
Incentive plan may not achieve the projected 5% and 2% reductions if root cause is prevalence rather than practice patterns
Focusing only on cardiac referrals leaves other high-cost specialty areas unaddressed
next_steps: Audit internal cardiology referral data and compare prevalence to U.S. national benchmarks
Interview Magna PCPs and external specialists to confirm referral pattern drivers
Benchmark specialist contract rates against Sunshine and industry averages
Launch physician incentive pilot and track referral rates and patient outcomes quarterly
Extend analysis to neurosurgery and oncology referral costs
